case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the 60-day deadline to petition the Federal Circuit for review of an MSPB decision under 5 U.S.C. § 7703(b)(1)(A) is a jurisdictional limit (blocking late filings categorically) or a nonjurisdictional claim-processing rule that can be equitably tolled.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 5 U.S.C. § 7703(b)(1)(A) (60-day time limit to seek Federal Circuit review of a Merits Systems Protection Board order/decision), with related structural context from 28 U.S.C. § 1295(a)(9) (Federal Circuit jurisdiction over MSPB petitions).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioner argues the 60-day limit in § 7703(b)(1)(A) is not jurisdictional because Congress did not make a clear statement tying timeliness to the Federal Circuit’s adjudicatory authority; under the Supreme Court’s modern 'clear statement' framework, filing deadlines are presumptively nonjurisdictional claim-processing rules and may allow equitable tolling in appropriate circumstances. Petitioner also contends the Federal Circuit’s contrary rule rests on outdated 'mandatory and jurisdictional' formulations and improper reliance on older circuit precedent and generalized statements about appeal deadlines rather than a text-and-structure-based jurisdictional analysis.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondent (Department of Defense/United States) argues the 60-day time limit is jurisdictional and therefore not subject to equitable tolling, relying on the statutory scheme governing judicial review of MSPB decisions, longstanding Federal Circuit precedent treating § 7703(b)(1)(A) as 'mandatory and jurisdictional,' and Supreme Court authority emphasizing that certain appeal-filing deadlines are jurisdictional. Under this view, an untimely petition deprives the Federal Circuit of power to hear the case regardless of equitable considerations.
key_precedents: Hamer v. Neighborhood Housing Services of Chicago, 583 U.S. 17 (2017)
Arbaugh v. Y & H Corp., 546 U.S. 500 (2006)
Fedora v. Merit Systems Protection Board, 848 F.3d 1013 (Fed. Cir. 2017)
Monzo v. Department of Transportation, 735 F.2d 1335 (Fed. Cir. 1984)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito’s strongest point is the structural linkage: § 1295(a)(9) authorizes review only “as authorized by” § 7703, and § 7703(b)(1)(A) says a petition “shall be filed” within 60 days, so timeliness is a condition on the court’s authority under Bowles. But Henderson and Hamer require more than a cross-reference plus mandatory timing language; they demand a clear statement that untimeliness strips adjudicatory power, and here Congress placed the jurisdictional grant in a separate Title 28 provision while § 7703(b)(1)(A) reads like an ordinary claim-processing directive. Bowles is best confined to the court-to-court appellate transfer setting (as Henderson/Hamer caution), and extending it to agency-review deadlines would revive the “drive-by jurisdiction” errors those cases sought to correct. Monzo/Fedora’s “mandatory and jurisdictional” labels, though cited by Justice Alito, predate the clarified framework and cannot supply Congress’s missing clear statement; a narrow holding that the deadline is nonjurisdictional while leaving tolling to demanding, traditional standards preserves finality and institutional legitimacy.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s strongest point is that Arbaugh/Hamer require a “clear statement” and that § 7703(b)(1)(A) lacks the word “jurisdiction,” but that modern canon cannot displace the statute’s original public meaning and the way Congress structured this particular review scheme. Read together, § 1295(a)(9)’s grant over petitions filed “pursuant to/ in accordance with” § 7703 and § 7703(b)(1)(A)’s command that a petition “shall be filed within 60 days” makes timeliness a condition precedent to invoking the court’s statutorily conferred authority, fitting Bowles’s treatment of congressionally set appeal deadlines as jurisdictional. Henderson and Hamer, as Roberts and Barrett note, caution against “drive-by jurisdiction,” but they do not justify recharacterizing a legislatively prescribed gateway to a specific tribunal as merely a claim-processing rule where the jurisdictional grant is expressly tied to compliance with the incorporated procedure. Justice Alito’s point about the channeling and finality interests in this personnel-review scheme reinforces that, absent any textual basis for tolling, an untimely petition must be dismissed for want of jurisdiction.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan rely on Arbaugh/Hamer’s clear-statement framework and the absence of the word “jurisdiction” in § 7703(b)(1)(A), but that approach gives too little weight to how Congress tied the Federal Circuit’s authority in § 1295(a)(9) to petitions brought “pursuant to” § 7703. When the very jurisdictional grant is limited to the class of petitions authorized by § 7703, the 60-day “shall be filed” requirement functions as a statutory condition on invoking the court’s power, making Bowles the closer analogue than Henderson/Hamer’s cautionary “drive-by” cases about court-made rules. Justice Sotomayor’s fairness and pro se concerns are serious, yet under a textualist and administrability-focused view they cannot justify equitable tolling where Congress prescribed a firm deadline as part of a channeling scheme for federal personnel litigation. Pre-Arbaugh Federal Circuit labels (Monzo; Fedora) are not dispositive, but they reinforce that the deadline has long been treated as a jurisdictional gateway consistent with the statutory structure.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito’s strongest point—that § 1295(a)(9)’s cross-reference to review “pursuant to/as authorized by” § 7703 makes § 7703(b)(1)(A)’s 60-day limit a condition on the Federal Circuit’s power—still fails under our clear-statement framework: “shall be filed within 60 days” is mandatory, but it does not speak in jurisdictional terms or specify that untimeliness strips adjudicatory authority. As Justice Kagan notes, the jurisdictional grant sits separately in § 1295(a)(9), which cuts against treating the timing directive in § 7703(b)(1)(A) as jurisdictional by implication. Bowles, emphasized by Justice Alito, is best confined (per Henderson and Hamer) to the Article III court-to-court appellate context; extending it to agency-review deadlines would revive the very drive-by jurisdiction mistakes we have been correcting. Given the access-to-justice stakes for often pro se federal employees, treating the deadline as a claim-processing rule preserves narrow equitable tolling without undermining routine enforcement or finality.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito press the strongest structural point: § 1295(a)(9) ties Federal Circuit review to what is “authorized by” (or “pursuant to”) § 7703, so the 60-day requirement should be a condition on the court’s power. But under Arbaugh/Henderson/Hamer, that kind of cross-reference plus “shall be filed … within 60 days” is still not a clear statement that untimeliness strips adjudicatory authority, especially because Congress located the jurisdictional grant in Title 28 and placed the timing directive separately in § 7703(b)(1)(A) without jurisdictional consequence language. Bowles does not move me because, as Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, it is best confined to Article III court-to-court appellate transfer settings; extending it to this agency-review scheme would revive the pre-Arbaugh practice of treating mandatory deadlines as jurisdictional by implication. Monzo/Fedora, invoked by Justice Alito, underscore administrability interests but cannot supply Congress’s missing clear statement, so the better textual reading remains a mandatory claim-processing rule with equitable tolling available only in narrow, traditional circumstances.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito are right to press the structural point that § 1295(a)(9) ties Federal Circuit review to what is “authorized by” (or “pursuant to”) § 7703, but that linkage still does not supply the clear textual signal our cases require to treat a filing deadline as jurisdictional. As the Chief Justice and Justice Barrett emphasize, § 7703(b)(1)(A) uses mandatory timing language (“shall be filed within 60 days”) yet omits any jurisdictional terms or express consequence that untimeliness strips the court of adjudicatory power; under Arbaugh and Hamer, that is decisive, and we should not infer jurisdictional effect by cross-reference alone. Bowles does not dislodge that conclusion because Henderson/Hamer confine it to the distinctive court-to-court appellate context where Congress regulates the transfer of Article III authority, whereas this is agency-to-court review with a separate jurisdictional grant in Title 28. The Federal Circuit’s Monzo/Fedora labels cannot substitute for Congress’s own words, and if Congress wished to make timeliness a jurisdictional prerequisite here, it could have said so plainly.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Alito’s and Justice Thomas’s strongest point is the structural linkage: § 1295(a)(9) grants Federal Circuit jurisdiction only over review “pursuant to” § 7703, and § 7703(b)(1)(A) says a petition “shall be filed” within 60 days, so timeliness is a condition on the court’s authority. But under Arbaugh/Hamer—as Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes—mandatory timing language plus a cross-reference still does not clearly state that untimeliness strips adjudicatory power, especially where Congress located the jurisdictional grant in Title 28 and omitted jurisdictional terminology or an express jurisdictional consequence in § 7703(b)(1)(A). Bowles is the closest precedent for Respondent, yet Henderson and Hamer cabin Bowles to court-to-court appellate deadlines and warn against reviving “drive-by” jurisdictional characterizations; extending Bowles to agency-review schemes absent an unmistakable congressional command would undercut that settled framework and the Court’s institutional clarity. Federal Circuit labels in Monzo/Fedora may reflect past practice, but they predate our clear-statement doctrine and cannot supply the missing congressional instruction; equitable tolling can remain narrow to preserve finality and administrability.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito’s strongest point—that § 1295(a)(9)’s jurisdictional grant is limited to petitions brought “pursuant to” or “as authorized by” § 7703, making § 7703(b)(1)(A)’s 60-day “shall be filed” language a jurisdictional condition—takes the statutory structure seriously, but it still does not supply the clear textual hook tying untimeliness to adjudicatory power that Arbaugh/Hamer demand. As Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, Congress placed the jurisdictional grant in Title 28 and used § 7703(b)(1)(A) to prescribe timing without jurisdictional terms or an express consequence (e.g., “no court shall have jurisdiction” or “the court shall dismiss for lack of jurisdiction”), which cuts against reading the deadline as jurisdictional even under a textualist lens sensitive to placement and drafting conventions. Bowles, relied on by Justices Thomas and Alito, is best confined—as Henderson and Hamer instruct—to the court-to-court appellate setting where Congress is explicitly regulating transfer of Article III adjudicatory authority; extending Bowles to agency-review timing provisions would risk reintroducing jurisdiction by implication. Federal Circuit precedent like Monzo/Fedora cannot supply Congress’s missing clear statement, so the deadline is a mandatory claim-processing rule subject to equitable tolling in narrow, traditional circumstances.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito press the best structural point—that § 1295(a)(9)’s grant of Federal Circuit jurisdiction is linked to petitions filed “pursuant to” § 7703, and § 7703(b)(1)(A) says the petition “shall be filed within 60 days,” so timeliness is a condition on authority. But under Arbaugh and Hamer, mandatory timing language plus a cross-reference still does not amount to the clear congressional statement needed to make a rule jurisdictional, especially where (as the Chief Justice notes) the jurisdictional grant sits in Title 28 and the time limit appears separately without jurisdictional terms or an express consequence of power-stripping. Bowles does not genuinely undermine that conclusion in my view because, as Justice Kagan emphasizes, Henderson/Hamer confine Bowles to the distinct court-to-court appellate-transfer context, whereas agency-to-court review deadlines carry a stronger presumption of nonjurisdictionality absent explicit text. Treating the deadline as a claim-processing rule better serves procedural fairness by preserving narrow equitable tolling for truly exceptional cases, while still allowing the Government to insist on timeliness when properly raised.

John Roberts.reasoning: Under this Court’s modern clear-statement framework, a filing deadline is treated as jurisdictional only if Congress clearly ties it to the court’s adjudicatory authority. Section 7703(b)(1)(A) sets a 60-day time limit to seek review of an MSPB decision, but it does not speak in jurisdictional terms or expressly condition the Federal Circuit’s power under 28 U.S.C. § 1295(a)(9) on timeliness, making it a nonjurisdictional claim-processing rule under Arbaugh and Hamer. Bowles involved a statutorily prescribed time limit for taking an appeal from one Article III court to another, a context Hamer distinguishes from agency-to-court review deadlines like this one. Respect for precedent and institutional legitimacy is best served by applying the Court’s settled jurisdictionality doctrine and permitting equitable tolling only in appropriate, narrowly cabined circumstances rather than imposing a categorical jurisdictional bar.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text and structure of the judicial-review scheme indicate Congress imposed a firm jurisdictional boundary: 28 U.S.C. § 1295(a)(9) grants the Federal Circuit jurisdiction over MSPB petitions only as authorized by 5 U.S.C. § 7703, and § 7703(b)(1)(A) specifies that such a petition "shall be filed" within 60 days. Under Bowles v. Russell, congressionally prescribed deadlines that condition access to an appellate tribunal function as limits on adjudicatory authority, and courts lack power to create equitable exceptions. Unlike purely internal claim-processing rules, this deadline is part of the statutory grant governing when judicial review may be invoked, and longstanding Federal Circuit precedent (e.g., Monzo; Fedora) properly treats it as mandatory and jurisdictional. Because Congress set the time for invoking the court’s review, an untimely petition must be dismissed for lack of jurisdiction.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 7703(b)(1)(A) states in mandatory terms that a petition for review “shall be filed within 60 days” after the MSPB’s final decision, and that deadline is the condition Congress attached to invoking the Federal Circuit’s statutorily granted review authority in this administrative-appeal scheme, see 28 U.S.C. § 1295(a)(9). Under Bowles v. Russell, statutory time limits governing the initiation of appellate review have been treated as jurisdictional and not subject to equitable tolling, and there is no textual basis here for a judicially created exception. Unlike the veterans-benefits context in Henderson, this CSRA review provision is not written as a uniquely claimant-protective, nonjurisdictional regime; treating the deadline as jurisdictional promotes finality and administrability and avoids case-by-case tolling disputes that would burden the courts and the Government. Consistent with longstanding Federal Circuit precedent (e.g., Monzo; Fedora) and the practical need for clear, enforceable filing rules in federal personnel litigation, an untimely petition should be dismissed for lack of jurisdiction.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 7703(b)(1)(A) sets a 60-day filing deadline but does not clearly tie timeliness to the Federal Circuit’s adjudicatory power, and under Arbaugh’s clear-statement rule and Hamer’s presumption that filing deadlines are nonjurisdictional claim-processing rules, that omission means the limit should not be treated as jurisdictional. Bowles is best read narrowly as involving appeals from one Article III court to another, whereas this deadline governs review of an agency board (the MSPB) under the jurisdictional grant in 28 U.S.C. § 1295(a)(9), making it more like the nonjurisdictional deadline in Henderson and thus amenable to equitable tolling. Treating § 7703(b)(1)(A) as nonjurisdictional preserves fairness and access to judicial review for federal employees—often facing resource and counsel disparities—while still permitting courts to enforce the deadline absent equitable grounds. Longstanding Federal Circuit labels like “mandatory and jurisdictional” (e.g., Monzo; Fedora) cannot substitute for Congress’s required clear statement under this Court’s modern framework.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 7703(b)(1)(A) sets a 60-day filing deadline but does not clearly tie that timing requirement to the Federal Circuit’s adjudicatory power; under the Court’s post-Arbaugh clear-statement approach, such deadlines are presumptively nonjurisdictional claim-processing rules unless Congress speaks in jurisdictional terms. The jurisdictional grant appears separately in 28 U.S.C. § 1295(a)(9), and § 7703(b)(1)(A)’s text reads like a timing directive (“must be filed … within 60 days”) rather than a limitation on subject-matter jurisdiction. Bowles v. Russell is best read, as Henderson and Hamer explain, as addressing statutory deadlines governing the transfer of authority between Article III courts; review of an MSPB order is not an appeal from one Article III court to another, so Bowles does not supply a categorical rule here. Given the statutory structure and the workability benefits of permitting equitable tolling in appropriate cases, I would treat the deadline as nonjurisdictional.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 7703(b)(1)(A) sets a 60-day deadline, but it does not clearly state that untimeliness strips the Federal Circuit of adjudicatory power; under Arbaugh v. Y & H Corp. and Hamer v. Neighborhood Housing Services, courts treat such deadlines as nonjurisdictional absent a clear congressional statement. The jurisdictional grant appears separately in 28 U.S.C. § 1295(a)(9), reinforcing that § 7703(b)(1)(A) is a claim-processing rule rather than a limit on subject-matter jurisdiction. Bowles v. Russell is best read, as Henderson indicates, as confined to the distinct context of statutory deadlines for appeals from one Article III court to another, not agency-to-court review like MSPB petitions. Because Congress did not “clearly” attach jurisdictional consequences here, equitable tolling remains available in appropriate cases.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Under this Court’s modern clear-statement framework, filing deadlines are presumptively nonjurisdictional unless Congress clearly ties the time bar to the court’s adjudicatory authority. Section 7703(b)(1)(A) sets a 60-day deadline but does not speak in jurisdictional terms or purport to limit the Federal Circuit’s jurisdiction granted in 28 U.S.C. § 1295(a)(9), making it better understood as a claim-processing rule subject to equitable tolling. Bowles v. Russell is best read, as Hamer explains, as confined to statutorily prescribed deadlines governing the transfer of adjudicatory authority between Article III courts, and it does not compel a jurisdictional label for administrative-review deadlines like this one. Although the Federal Circuit’s older precedent (e.g., Monzo; Fedora) treated the deadline as “mandatory and jurisdictional,” that phrasing predates Arbaugh’s and Hamer’s clarified approach and cannot substitute for a clear congressional statement.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Under the Court’s clear-statement framework, a time limit is jurisdictional only if Congress clearly ties it to the court’s adjudicatory authority. Section 7703(b)(1)(A) sets a 60-day deadline for seeking Federal Circuit review but does not speak in jurisdictional terms or condition the Federal Circuit’s power under 28 U.S.C. § 1295(a)(9) on timely filing, making it a nonjurisdictional claim-processing rule. Bowles v. Russell treated certain court-to-court appeal deadlines as jurisdictional, but Henderson and Hamer confine that rationale and reiterate that most filing deadlines—especially outside the Article III-to-Article III appellate context—are not jurisdictional absent a clear statement. Because § 7703(b)(1)(A) concerns review of an administrative board decision and lacks a clear jurisdictional command, it is subject to equitable tolling in appropriate cases notwithstanding contrary Federal Circuit precedent like Fedora.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Under this Court’s clear-statement framework, filing deadlines are presumptively nonjurisdictional unless Congress clearly ties the time limit to the court’s adjudicatory power. Section 7703(b)(1)(A) sets a 60-day deadline but does not speak in jurisdictional terms or condition the Federal Circuit’s jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1295(a)(9) on timely filing, making it a claim-processing rule subject to equitable tolling in appropriate cases. Bowles v. Russell is best confined to statutes that expressly link timing to a jurisdictional grant, while Hamer and Arbaugh instruct that courts should not treat time limits as jurisdictional absent clear statutory language. Treating § 7703(b)(1)(A) as nonjurisdictional also advances procedural fairness in a system where MSPB appellants are often pro se and the practical consequences of categorical dismissal can be severe.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the 60-day deadline to seek Federal Circuit review of a Merit Systems Protection Board decision under the Civil Service Reform Act is a jurisdictional limit (thus barring late filings regardless of excuse) or a nonjurisdictional claim-processing rule subject to equitable tolling.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 5 U.S.C. § 7703(b)(1)(A) (60-day time limit to file a petition for review of an MSPB final order/decision in the Federal Circuit).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioner argues the 60-day deadline in § 7703(b)(1)(A) is not jurisdictional because Congress did not clearly state that the timing rule limits the Federal Circuit’s adjudicatory power. Under the Supreme Court’s modern 'clear statement' approach, ordinary filing deadlines are presumptively nonjurisdictional claim-processing rules, and late filing should not automatically defeat subject-matter jurisdiction. Therefore, the deadline should be subject to equitable tolling in appropriate circumstances, and Federal Circuit precedent labeling it 'mandatory and jurisdictional' relies on outdated terminology and pre-clear-statement analysis (and an overreading of appeal-deadline cases like Bowles). Amici further contend that treating the deadline as jurisdictional is especially unfair in the MSPB context, where many appellants are pro se (including veterans), and argue that even if ambiguity exists, interpretive principles (including a veteran-friendly canon urged by one amicus) favor allowing tolling.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondent (United States/Department of Defense) argues the 60-day time limit in § 7703(b)(1)(A) is jurisdictional and therefore not subject to equitable tolling. On this view, Congress set a firm condition on the Federal Circuit’s authority to review MSPB decisions, and the court of appeals correctly dismissed untimely petitions for lack of jurisdiction. The government relies on the statutory structure governing Federal Circuit review and the Federal Circuit’s longstanding line of cases treating the deadline as jurisdictional, contending that this context indicates Congress intended strict enforcement without equitable exceptions.
key_precedents: Hamer v. Neighborhood Housing Services of Chicago, 583 U.S. 17 (2017)
Fedora v. Merit Systems Protection Board, 848 F.3d 1013 (Fed. Cir. 2017) (including Plager, J., dissenting; referenced by amici)
Monzo v. Department of Transportation, 735 F.2d 1335 (Fed. Cir. 1984)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito are right to press Bowles, the CSRA’s channeling structure, and the Federal Circuit’s Monzo line as evidence of a traditionally strict gatekeeping deadline, but under our post-Arbaugh/Hamer framework that history cannot substitute for a clear congressional statement tying timeliness to adjudicatory power. Unlike Bowles’s distinctive Article III-to-Article III notice-of-appeal regime, § 7703(b)(1)(A) is party-directed (“shall be filed within 60 days”) and does not condition the Federal Circuit’s jurisdictional grant in § 1295(a)(9) on compliance, which is the textual link our cases demand. Justice Sotomayor and Justice Kagan’s Henderson/Irwin points reinforce that in this administrative-review setting, absent a clear contrary command, we should treat the deadline as a mandatory but nonjurisdictional claim-processing rule, leaving tolling and other equitable questions for ordinary standards on remand. A narrow holding limited to characterization preserves settled enforcement in the run of cases while avoiding the harsh, nonwaivable consequences that the jurisdictional label would impose without Congress speaking clearly.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: I remain unpersuaded by Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s reliance on our post-Arbaugh “clear-statement” cases and Irwin’s tolling presumption because those judge-made frameworks cannot displace the enacted text and the traditional understanding of congressionally prescribed time limits for invoking appellate review. Section 7703(b)(1)(A) provides that a petition “shall be filed within 60 days,” and in the CSRA’s tightly channeled review scheme that language is best read as a condition on the availability of the Federal Circuit’s review, not a mere case-management directive. Justice Sotomayor’s effort to confine Bowles to Article III-to-Article III appeals overlooks that Congress similarly specified the temporal terms on which this statutorily created path of review may be invoked; absent statutory authorization, courts have no equitable power to relax that prerequisite. Henderson’s solicitude-driven reasoning in the veterans context does not translate to this adversarial civil-service regime, and the Federal Circuit’s longstanding construction (Monzo), while not controlling, accords with the statute’s original public meaning and structure.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: I am not persuaded by Chief Justice Roberts’s Arbaugh/Hamer clear-statement framing because it treats § 7703(b)(1)(A) as a generic filing rule rather than a condition embedded in the CSRA’s exclusive, tightly channeled avenue of judicial review, where Congress reasonably demanded prompt finality and where the 60-day command functions as a prerequisite to the Federal Circuit’s authority to entertain the petition. Justice Sotomayor’s reliance on Henderson does not move me: Henderson’s nonadversarial, veteran-friendly scheme is a poor analogue to the CSRA’s structured, adversarial regime, so the “harsh consequences” concern cannot override the statutory design choice for strict gatekeeping. Justice Kagan’s invocation of Irwin’s tolling presumption also seems inapt here because the relevant question is not merely whether tolling is sometimes available against the Government, but whether Congress made timely invocation a condition of the reviewing court’s power in this particular review path—an inquiry that Bowles and the long-settled Federal Circuit understanding (as Justice Thomas notes) reinforce. The opposing side’s strongest point is that § 7703(b)(1)(A) does not use the word “jurisdiction,” but under my methodology that absence is not dispositive when the time limit is integral to the statutory grant of review in an exclusive scheme and has been treated as such for decades.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito’s strongest point is the CSRA’s channeled review structure plus Bowles and Monzo, suggesting Congress meant the 60-day limit as a condition on the Federal Circuit’s power. But under the Court’s modern clear-statement rule, that structural intuition and historical labeling cannot substitute for what Congress actually said: as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, § 7703(b)(1)(A) is party-directed (“shall be filed within 60 days”) and does not textually condition the jurisdictional grant in § 1295(a)(9) or use jurisdictional terms. Alito’s attempt to distinguish Henderson as “veterans-only” doesn’t answer Henderson’s broader caution against expanding Bowles beyond the Article III notice-of-appeal context, where the jurisdictional label creates uniquely harsh, nonwaivable forfeitures. Irwin’s presumption, highlighted by Justice Kagan, reinforces that absent a clear contrary command we should not read this deadline to slam the courthouse door on federal employees—often unrepresented—where equitable principles may warrant tolling in extraordinary cases.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito are right to press Bowles and the CSRA’s “tightly channeled” review scheme, but under our post-Arbaugh/Hamer framework that history does not substitute for a clear textual link between the 60-day limit and the Federal Circuit’s adjudicatory power. As the Chief Justice and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, § 7703(b)(1)(A) is litigant-directed (“shall be filed within 60 days”) and does not condition the jurisdictional grant in 28 U.S.C. § 1295(a)(9) on timeliness or use jurisdictional terms, which is the decisive feature in our disciplined jurisdictionality cases. Bowles is best confined to the distinctive Article III notice-of-appeal regime; extending it here would dilute the clear-statement rule and conflict with Henderson’s treatment of agency-review deadlines. And Monzo’s “mandatory and jurisdictional” label, highlighted by Justice Alito, predates that framework and cannot itself supply the clear congressional statement required, leaving the deadline mandatory but nonjurisdictional (with Irwin’s tolling presumption available only in extraordinary circumstances).

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s strongest point is Bowles and the traditional treatment of statutory appellate deadlines as jurisdictional, bolstered by the Federal Circuit’s Monzo line, but under our textualist/originalist discipline the question is what Congress enacted—not how lower courts once labeled it. As the Chief Justice and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, § 7703(b)(1)(A) is framed in party-directed terms (“shall be filed within 60 days”) and does not condition the Federal Circuit’s jurisdictional grant in 28 U.S.C. § 1295(a)(9) on timeliness or use jurisdictional language, which is the clear-statement linkage Arbaugh and Hamer require. Bowles is best read as confined to the historically distinctive notice-of-appeal regime between Article III courts; extending it here would dilute the clarity those cases demand and risk turning many mandatory filing rules into jurisdictional traps without textual warrant. Justice Alito’s structural/finality concerns may justify strict enforcement as a claim-processing rule, but they cannot supply the missing statutory command that would make the deadline nonwaivable and jurisdiction-stripping.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito’s best point is that § 7703(b)(1)(A) sits in a tightly channeled review scheme and has long been treated as “mandatory and jurisdictional” (Monzo), echoing Bowles’s treatment of statutory appeal deadlines. But under our modern clear-statement framework (Arbaugh, Hamer), that history and the statute’s mandatory “shall” language are not enough without a textual link making timeliness a condition on the Federal Circuit’s adjudicatory power—especially where jurisdiction is granted separately in § 1295(a)(9) without any timeliness hook, as the Chief Justice stresses. Henderson’s caution about extending Bowles beyond the Article III notice-of-appeal context is persuasive here; treating this as nonjurisdictional preserves the ordinary strict enforcement of the 60-day rule while avoiding the uniquely harsh, nonwaivable consequences of a jurisdictional label. I remain comfortable leaving tolling’s availability to ordinary equitable principles on remand rather than baking in an across-the-board jurisdictional bar.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito are right to press Bowles and the CSRA’s channeled review structure, but under our textualist, clear-statement framework, mandatory language (“shall be filed within 60 days”) does not itself transform a time limit into a limit on adjudicatory power. As the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, § 7703(b)(1)(A) is party-directed and lacks jurisdictional terms or any textual linkage to the Federal Circuit’s jurisdictional grant in 28 U.S.C. § 1295(a)(9), which Arbaugh and Hamer treat as decisive. Bowles is best read narrowly in its Article III-to-Article III notice-of-appeal setting, and Henderson counsels against reflexively extending jurisdictional consequences to administrative-review deadlines absent clearer statutory direction. The Federal Circuit’s older Monzo line, invoked by Justice Alito, cannot supply Congress’s missing clear statement, though it may bear on how strictly the claim-processing rule is ordinarily enforced and whether equitable tolling should be rare.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s Bowles-based argument is the hardest pushback because it invokes a tradition of treating statutory filing deadlines as jurisdictional, but our modern doctrine rejects categorical rules and instead demands a clear congressional statement tying the deadline to adjudicatory power. As the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, § 7703(b)(1)(A) is party-directed (“shall be filed within 60 days”) and does not condition the Federal Circuit’s jurisdictional grant in § 1295(a)(9) on timeliness, which is decisive under Arbaugh/Hamer and consistent with Henderson’s reluctance to extend Bowles beyond the Article III notice-of-appeal context. Justice Alito’s reliance on Monzo and congressional silence is real contextual evidence, but precedent labels and acquiescence cannot supply the missing clear statement—especially where Irwin supports a tolling presumption in suits involving the United States. Treating the provision as a mandatory claim-processing rule preserves the 60-day requirement in ordinary cases while avoiding unnecessarily harsh forfeiture when equity truly warrants.

John Roberts.reasoning: Under this Court’s clear-statement framework, a statutory time bar is jurisdictional only if Congress clearly ties it to the court’s adjudicatory power; absent such language, it is treated as a nonjurisdictional claim-processing rule. Section 7703(b)(1)(A) sets a 60-day filing deadline but does not speak in jurisdictional terms or condition the Federal Circuit’s subject-matter jurisdiction on timeliness, which makes it unlike the appeal deadline treated as jurisdictional in Bowles v. Russell. Consistent with Arbaugh v. Y&H Corp. and Hamer v. Neighborhood Housing Services, the better reading is that the deadline is mandatory but not jurisdictional and thus presumptively subject to equitable tolling in appropriate cases. A narrow holding—limited to the jurisdictional characterization, leaving tolling’s application to ordinary equitable principles—promotes coherence in our jurisdictional doctrine and institutional legitimacy without unsettling merits outcomes.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text of 5 U.S.C. § 7703(b)(1)(A) sets a firm condition—“any petition for review shall be filed within 60 days”—on the availability of Federal Circuit review of an MSPB final decision, and nothing in the statute authorizes equitable tolling. Under Bowles v. Russell, 551 U.S. 205 (2007), when Congress sets a statutory time limit for invoking an appellate tribunal’s review, courts lack authority to create equitable exceptions inconsistent with that limit. The Civil Service Reform Act channels review to a specific court on specified terms, and longstanding Federal Circuit precedent treating § 7703(b)(1)(A) as jurisdictional (e.g., Monzo v. Dep’t of Transp., 735 F.2d 1335 (Fed. Cir. 1984)) accords with that original understanding of Congress’s limits on the courts’ power. Whatever this Court’s later “clear statement” cases (e.g., Arbaugh; Hamer) suggest as a policy matter, the enacted text and the historically strict treatment of statutory appeal-filing deadlines counsel treating this time bar as jurisdictional and not subject to equitable tolling.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 7703(b)(1)(A) sets out a firm, statute-based 60-day limit for invoking Federal Circuit review of MSPB decisions, and in this setting Congress plausibly made timeliness a condition on the court’s authority to entertain the petition. In Bowles v. Russell, this Court treated statutory appeal deadlines as jurisdictional where they function to channel review in a tightly cabined appellate scheme, and the CSRA’s review provisions reflect a similarly structured, consequence-sensitive regime that benefits from clear, enforceable cutoffs. While Arbaugh and Hamer emphasize a clear-statement approach, they also preserve the traditional treatment of statutorily prescribed appellate filing periods, and longstanding Federal Circuit precedent (e.g., Monzo) has consistently read § 7703(b)(1)(A) as “mandatory and jurisdictional,” which Congress has left undisturbed. Given the practical consequences for finality and the orderly administration of the civil service system, I would adhere to that settled understanding and hold the deadline jurisdictional and not subject to equitable tolling.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Under this Court’s modern clear-statement framework, a statutory filing deadline is jurisdictional only if Congress clearly indicates it limits the court’s adjudicatory power, and 5 U.S.C. § 7703(b)(1)(A) contains no such unmistakable jurisdictional language. As in Arbaugh v. Y&H Corp. and Hamer v. Neighborhood Housing Services, the 60-day limit is best understood as a nonjurisdictional claim-processing rule, which ordinarily remains subject to equitable tolling when fairness so requires. Bowles v. Russell does not compel a contrary result because it addressed a distinct category—appeals from one Article III court to another—where Congress historically imposed jurisdictional constraints, whereas this provision governs review of an administrative board decision and resembles the veterans’ appeal deadline found tollable in Henderson. Treating § 7703(b)(1)(A) as jurisdictional would needlessly and harshly foreclose review for often pro se federal employees (including veterans) despite reasonable excuses, undermining access to justice without any clear congressional command.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 7703(b)(1)(A) sets a 60-day deadline to file a petition for review, but it does not clearly state that the timing requirement limits the Federal Circuit’s adjudicatory power; under Arbaugh and Hamer, that absence of a clear jurisdictional label and jurisdiction-tying language means the deadline is presumptively a nonjurisdictional claim-processing rule. Irwin adds a further presumption that statutory filing deadlines involving the United States are subject to equitable tolling absent a contrary clear statement, and nothing in § 7703(b)(1)(A)’s text supplies the kind of unmistakable jurisdictional command found in truly jurisdictional regimes. Bowles does not compel a different result because it addressed a distinct, historically jurisdictional notice-of-appeal deadline in a different statutory setting, and our modern cases caution against extending that treatment without Congress’s clear statement. Treating the deadline as nonjurisdictional preserves statutory coherence and workability by allowing tolling only in appropriate cases while still enforcing the 60-day rule in the mine-run of MSPB appeals.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 7703(b)(1)(A) sets a 60-day filing deadline but does not clearly state that untimeliness strips the Federal Circuit of adjudicatory authority, and under this Court’s clear-statement rule ordinary time limits are presumptively nonjurisdictional claim-processing rules. As in Arbaugh and Hamer, we should not attach “jurisdictional” consequences absent unmistakable statutory text; the provision speaks in terms of what a party must do (“shall be filed”) rather than delineating the court’s power. Bowles is best read as limited to the distinctive statutory notice-of-appeal regime long treated as jurisdictional, and Henderson teaches that context and clarity matter—here the text and structure do not clearly incorporate the deadline into the jurisdictional grant. Because the deadline is nonjurisdictional, it may be subject to equitable tolling in appropriate cases.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Under this Court’s modern clear-statement framework, statutory filing deadlines are presumptively nonjurisdictional claim-processing rules unless Congress clearly ties the deadline to the court’s adjudicatory power. Section 7703(b)(1)(A) sets a 60-day period to file in the Federal Circuit but does not state that untimely petitions deprive the court of jurisdiction, and the Federal Circuit’s jurisdictional grant in 28 U.S.C. § 1295(a)(9) is not textually conditioned on compliance with that deadline. Bowles v. Russell involved a distinct statutory scheme expressly treated as jurisdictional for civil appeals and does not create a categorical rule that all congressionally enacted deadlines are jurisdictional; Hamer and Arbaugh reinforce that jurisdictional labels require a clear statement. Treating § 7703(b)(1)(A) as nonjurisdictional preserves practical workability by allowing equitable tolling in truly extraordinary cases without undermining the statutory deadline’s ordinary enforcement.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 7703(b)(1)(A) provides that a petition for review “shall be filed within 60 days,” but it does not clearly speak in jurisdictional terms or tie the time limit to the Federal Circuit’s adjudicatory power, which this Court’s clear-statement framework requires. Under Arbaugh v. Y&H Corp. and Hamer v. Neighborhood Housing Services, ordinary statutory filing deadlines are presumptively nonjurisdictional claim-processing rules unless Congress clearly indicates otherwise, and the text and placement of § 7703(b)(1)(A) do not supply that indication. Bowles v. Russell is best cabined to congressionally prescribed deadlines for appeals from one Article III court to another, not agency-to-court review like MSPB petitions, consistent with Henderson v. Shinseki’s treatment of similar administrative-review deadlines. Federal Circuit precedent labeling the deadline “mandatory and jurisdictional” predates (and is in tension with) the Court’s modern methodology, so the time limit should be treated as nonjurisdictional and potentially subject to equitable tolling.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 7703(b)(1)(A)’s 60-day deadline is best read as a nonjurisdictional claim-processing rule because Congress did not clearly state that the timing requirement limits the Federal Circuit’s adjudicatory power, as required by Arbaugh’s clear-statement framework and reaffirmed in Hamer. Bowles does not compel a jurisdictional label here because it involved a congressionally prescribed appeal deadline from one Article III court to another, whereas § 7703(b)(1)(A) governs judicial review of an administrative board decision, a context where this Court has been reluctant to attach the “harsh consequences” of jurisdictionality absent clear indication (see Henderson). Treating the deadline as nonjurisdictional preserves procedural fairness by allowing equitable tolling in rare, appropriate cases without undermining the statute’s general insistence on prompt review.
